Let's load the AirBnB dataset downloaded from [here](https://public.opendatasoft.com/explore/dataset/airbnb-listings/export/?disjunctive.host_verifications&disjunctive.amenities&disjunctive.features&q=Madrid&%3D&location=16,41.38377,2.15774&basemap=jawg.streets)

![](download.png)

```{r}
airbnb<-read.csv("C:/Users/adril/Downloads/airbnb-listings.csv",sep = ';')
options(repr.plot.height=4,repr.plot.width=6,repr.plot.res = 300)
```

1.  Let's keep the most relevant columns.: 'City','Room.Type','Neighbourhood','Accommodates','Bathrooms','Bedrooms','Beds','Price','Square.Feet','Guests.Included','Extra.People','Review.Scores.Rating','Latitude', 'Longitude' Nos quedarmos solo con las entradas de Madrid para Room.Type=="Entire home/apt" y cuyo barrio (Neighbourhood) no está vacio '' Podemos eliminar las siguientes columnas que ya no son necesarias: "Room.Type",'City' Llama a nuevo dataframe df_madrid.

```{r}
df_madrid<- airbnb[which(airbnb$City == "Madrid" & airbnb$Room.Type=="Entire home/apt" & airbnb$Neighbourhood!=""), c('Neighbourhood','Accommodates','Bathrooms','Bedrooms','Beds','Price','Square.Feet','Guests.Included','Extra.People','Review.Scores.Rating','Latitude',  'Longitude')]
```

```{r}
df_madrid
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

2.  Create a new column called Square.Meters from Square.Feet. Remember that one square foot is 0.092903 square meters..

```{r}
df_madrid$Square.Meters<-df_madrid$Square.Feet*0.092903
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

3.  What percentage of the apartments do not show the square meters? That is, how many have NA in Square.Meters?

```{r}
#summary(df_madrid$Square.Meters)
valores_NA <- sum(length(which(is.na(df_madrid$Square.Meters))))
valores_totales <- sum(length(df_madrid$Square.Meters))
porcen_NA <- (valores_NA/valores_totales)*100
cat("El total de NAs es de", porcen_NA, "%.", "Hay un total de", valores_NA, "valores NA.")
valores_totales
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

4.  Of all the apartments with a non-NA square meter value, what percentage of them have 0 square meters?

```{r}
no_NA <- length(which(!is.na(df_madrid$Square.Meters)))
num_no_NA <- nrow(no_NA)
cerom2 <- length(which(df_madrid$Square.Meters==0))
porcen_cerom2 <- (cerom2/no_NA)*100
cat("El porcentaje de apartamentos no NA con 0 metros cuadrados es", porcen_cerom2, "%. El total de apartamentos con cero metros cuadrados es", cerom2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

5.  Replace all 0m² with NA.

```{r}
df_madrid$Square.Meters[df_madrid$Square.Meters == 0] <- NA
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

There are many NAs, so we're going to try to create a model that predicts the square meters based on the other variables in order to fill in those NAs. But before creating the model, we're going to:
* plot the histogram of the square meters to see if we need to filter out any additional elements.
* create a new synthetic variable based on the similarity between neighborhoods, which we’ll use in our model.

6.  Plot the histogram of the square meters and see if we need to filter out any additional elements

```{r}

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

square_meters_clean <- df_madrid |> filter(!is.na(Square.Meters))

ggplot(data=square_meters_clean, aes(x=Square.Meters))+
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill="#7070BB", color="#2020EE")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 500, 50), lim = c(0, 500)) +
  xlab("Square Meters")+ylab("Nº Apartments")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

7.  Assign the value NA to the Square.Meters column of the apartments that have less than 20 m²

```{r}
df_madrid$Square.Meters[df_madrid$Square.Meters<20]<-NA
```

    ```{r}
    library(dplyr)

    df_madrid <- df_madrid |> filter(Neighbourhood %in% df_neighbourhood$Neighbourhood)
    ```

9.  Do all neighborhoods have the same average square meters? Which test would you use to check that?

    ```{r}
    shapiro.test(df_madrid$Square.Meters)
    ```

```{r}
kruskal.test(df_madrid$Square.Meters ~ df_madrid$Neighbourhood, data = df_madrid)
```

10. "Let's group the neighborhoods based on square meters. We can use a Tukey similarity matrix. It shows how similar or different the neighborhoods are when we only consider the square meters of the apartments. How does the mean of Neighborhood A differ from Neighborhood B? (That is, what would be the p-value assuming a null hypothesis where the means are equal?)

    ```{r}

    df_madrid$Square.Meters.Scaled <- scale(df_madrid$Square.Meters)


    anova_result <- aov(Square.Meters.Scaled ~ Neighbourhood, data = df_madrid)
    summary(anova_result)

    tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(anova_result)
    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

11. In the previous step, you created a matrix of p-values that indicates how similar two neighborhoods are. If the p-value is low, it means the neighborhoods are different; if it's high, it means they are similar. We can use this matrix as a distance matrix by subtracting the p-value from 1 — that is, using 1 - p-value as the distance. In this way, neighborhoods with a high p-value will have a greater distance than those with a low p-value. Using this last metric as the distance matrix, draw a dendrogram of the different neighborhoods.

    ```{r}
    #crear matriz de distancia
    tky <- TukeyHSD(aov(Square.Meters ~ Neighbourhood, data = df_madrid))
    tky.result <- data.frame(tky$Neighbourhood)
    cn <- sort(unique(df_madrid$Neighbourhood))
    resm <- matrix(NA, length(cn), length(cn))
    rownames(resm) <- cn
    colnames(resm) <- cn
    resm[lower.tri(resm)] <- round(tky.result$p.adj, 4)
    resm[upper.tri(resm)] <- t(resm)[upper.tri(resm)]
    diag(resm) <- 1

    # crear grafica

    dist <- as.dist(1 - resm)
    hc <- hclust(dist, method = "average")
    plot(hc, main = "Dendrograma", xlab = "Neighbourhood", sub = "")
    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

11.1. What would be the recommended cut-off point? How many clusters appear?

```{r}
#Dado que el dendograma va desde 0 hasta 0.6, lo mejor sería realizar el cluster en su mitad en el 0.3 ya que en este punto no dejamos grupos demasiado grandes pero tampoco dividimos demasiado los grupos.

clusters <- cutree(hc, h = 0.3)

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

11. Let's create a new column in the df_madrid dataframe with a new identifier marked by the obtained clusters. We'll call this column neighb_id

    ```{r}
    df_madrid$neighb_id <- clusters[match(df_madrid$Neighbourhood, names(clusters))]

    df_madrid$neighb_id <- factor(df_madrid$neighb_id)

    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

12. Let's create two groups: one for testing and one for training.

    ```{r}
    set.seed(4321)

    idx <- sample(1:nrow(df_madrid), nrow(df_madrid) * 0.7)

    train <- df_madrid[idx, ]
    test <- df_madrid[-idx, ]
    train <- na.omit(train)
    test <- na.omit(test)
    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

13. We try to predict the square meters based on the other columns in the dataframe.

    ```{r}
    modelo <- lm(Square.Meters ~ Accommodates + Bathrooms + Price + Bedrooms + Beds + Review.Scores.Rating, data = train)

    summary(modelo)

    predicciones <- predict(modelo, newdata = test)
    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

14. Evaluate the quality of your model

    ```{r}
    library(caret)


    cat("La calidad del modelo en train es:
        ")
    train$pred <- predict(modelo, train)
    postResample(train$pred, obs = train$Square.Meters)

    cat("La calidad del modelo en predicciones es:
        ")
    postResample(predicciones, obs=test$Square.Meters)
    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

15. If we had a listing for an apartment that accommodates 6 people, with 1 bathroom, priced at €80 per night, with 3 bedrooms in the Sol neighborhood, with 3 beds and a review score of 80, how many square meters would it have? If your model needs any additional variable, you can make it up as long as it's within the dataset's value range. How does its square meterage change with each additional bedroom?

    ```{r}

    anuncio <- data.frame(Accommodates = 6,Bathrooms = 1,Price = 80,Bedrooms = 3,Beds = 3,Review.Scores.Rating = 80)

    pred_square_meters <- predict(modelo, newdata = anuncio)
    pred_square_meters

    #summary(modelo)

    #Since the coefficient for bedrooms is 19.25071 (which I saw in the summary of my model), every time we increase or decrease the number of bedrooms (while keeping the other variables constant), the square meters will vary by approximately 19.25 m² for each bedroom we add or remove.
    ```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

16. Fill the Square.Meters with NA values using the estimate from the previous model.

    ```{r}
    df.na <- df_madrid[is.na(df_madrid$Square.Meters), ]
    predict_con_na <- predict(modelo, newdata = df.na)


    df_madrid[is.na(df_madrid$Square.Meters), "Square.Meters"] <- predict_con_na
    ```

    ```{r}
    df_madrid
    ```
